concept.name: Drift
concept.definition: The deterministic, systematic component of a stochastic process - the average rate at which the process is expected to move per unit of time, distinct from its random fluctuations. In a geometric Brownian motion or random walk with drift, it is the constant expected change per period.
concept.intuition: Drift is the steady current in a river; the waves are random, but the current carries you in one direction on average.
concept.mechanics: In a random walk with drift X_t = c + X_{t-1} + epsilon_t, c is the drift and the process trends upward (or downward) by c per period on average. In continuous time, dS_t = mu*S_t*dt + sigma*S_t*dW_t has drift mu*S_t, the expected instantaneous return. Drift is estimated as a sample mean of increments and is hard to estimate precisely because estimation error shrinks only with the length of the time span, not the sampling frequency.
concept.formula: Random walk with drift: X_t = c + X_{t-1} + epsilon_t, so E[X_t - X_{t-1}] = c. GBM: dS_t = mu*S_t*dt + sigma*S_t*dW_t, with mu the drift (expected return).
concept.failure_modes: Drift estimates over short samples are extremely imprecise: decades of daily data still leave wide confidence intervals on annual expected returns. Assuming a constant drift fails when expected returns are time-varying or regime-dependent.
concept.misconceptions: That more frequent sampling (e.g., minute data) improves drift estimates - it does not, because drift uncertainty depends on the total time span; and that a visible trend in a short sample establishes a nonzero drift.
concept.example: U.S. equity prices are often modeled as a random walk with positive drift of roughly 6-8% per year, but estimating that drift from a 20-year sample carries a standard error of several percentage points.

citations.source: Wikipedia, Stochastic volatility (definition of drift in geometric Brownian motion)
